doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
title: Growing up in the Depression, steelworker father and unions
summary: Poor immigrant family in Martin's Ferry; his father was a union-minded steelworker and he recalls labor violence and politics.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: You would have been pretty young during the Depression.
Do you have any recollection of that being a particularly hard time for your family or your neighborhood?

Yeah well you know my parents were immigrants and we were poor but I didn’t know it. My mother was such a handy housekeeper and she cooked and cleaned and baked, and you know it was just sort of — and my father was a steel worker, he worked in the steel mill and stuff, and that was, I remember that was the era of the unions organizing you know, which was very critical. I mean today I know maybe unions are considered Mafia run and all that, but in my estimation there’s a great room in America for labor unions and what labor unions do. And so I remember when I had a friend who was very teary and crying and he said one day his father had been beaten to death by company goons with a baseball bat, because they wanted to strike or something like that. So I remember that and I remember my father was out on the left wing you know. I remember that he was very involved in politics in the sense of voting for somebody or campaigning for somebody you know. And there was a famous — well to me a famous — governor Davey I think it was, I don’t know I think in the 30s. And there was a lot of campaigning against him. And he had some sort of tar road plan and so on. And somehow he had something to swindle about tarring, making asphalt roads or whatever you know. So yes, I have a very strong and vivid memory of the Depression and to this day I love old movies made as contemporary movies in the 30s, and the earlier the better. They’re very interesting because they reflect the time. And I get that feeling from them.
